title: Media Literacy and Digital Texts
unitGoal: Students will interpret media messages, notice audience and purpose, evaluate digital information, and create responsible media responses.

lessons.title: What Is a Media Message?
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify media messages and explain what they are trying to communicate.
successCriteria: I can identify a media text.
I can explain the main message in a media text.
I can notice how words, images, and sounds work together.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise identifying media texts and explaining their main messages.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise identifying media texts and explaining their main messages.
lessonContent: A media text shares a message using words, images, sound, video, design, or a mix of these.
Posters, videos, websites, announcements, maps, labels, and advertisements are all media texts.
A media message is what the text wants the audience to notice, understand, feel, or do.
The words and images in a media text usually work together.
Careful readers look beyond the first impression and ask what message is being sent.

studentActivity.title: Media Message Detective
studentActivity.mission: Decide what different media texts are trying to communicate.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: media texts send messages
steps.text: Media is not only television or the internet. A school poster, a cereal box, a bus sign, a website button, or a church bulletin notice can all send a message.

steps.title: Ask What It Communicates
steps.prompt: Look for the main idea
steps.text: A media text may inform, invite, warn, explain, entertain, or persuade. To find the message, ask what the creator wants people to notice or do.

steps.title: Media Text
steps.prompt: Which item is a media text?
choices: a poster inviting families to a school open house
a folder used to carry school notices
a printer used to make classroom signs
steps.correctAnswer: a poster inviting families to a school open house
steps.feedback: Correct. The poster uses words and design to communicate.
steps.hint: Choose the item that sends a message to an audience.

steps.title: Main Message
steps.prompt: A poster says, 'Bring a reusable bottle on field trip day' and shows a bottle beside a backpack. What is the main message?
choices: Students should remember to bring a reusable bottle.
Students should choose a backpack with side pockets.
Field trips often include outdoor activities.
steps.correctAnswer: Students should remember to bring a reusable bottle.
steps.feedback: Yes. The words and picture point to that reminder.
steps.hint: Use both the words and image.

steps.title: Message Type
steps.prompt: A sign near a trail says, 'Stay on marked paths to protect plants.' What is the sign mostly doing?
choices: giving a safety and care instruction
advertising a new trail map
telling a story about plant growth
steps.correctAnswer: giving a safety and care instruction
steps.feedback: Correct. The sign tells people what to do and why.
steps.hint: Ask what action the sign wants.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A media text can use both words and images to send one clear message.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Words and images often work together.
steps.hint: Media messages can have several parts.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised identifying media messages.

steps.title: Read the Whole Message
steps.prompt: Images can change meaning
steps.text: A picture, colour, symbol, or layout can change how a message feels. A warning sign and a celebration poster may use very different design choices.

steps.title: Image Support
steps.prompt: A library poster says, 'Try a new book this week' and shows students choosing books from different shelves. How does the image help?
choices: It shows the action the poster is encouraging.
It gives the exact rules for borrowing books.
It explains how libraries buy new books.
steps.correctAnswer: It shows the action the poster is encouraging.
steps.feedback: Correct. The image supports the message.
steps.hint: Look for what the picture adds.

steps.title: Symbol
steps.prompt: A website uses a small magnifying glass icon beside a search box. What does the icon help users understand?
choices: where to search for information
how to change the website colours
which page was opened most recently
steps.correctAnswer: where to search for information
steps.feedback: Yes. The symbol gives a quick clue.
steps.hint: Think about common symbols.

steps.title: Best Message
steps.prompt: Which message best fits a school announcement that says, 'Concert tickets are available until Friday'?
choices: Families should get tickets before Friday.
Students should practise music every Friday.
The concert program will include many songs.
steps.correctAnswer: Families should get tickets before Friday.
steps.feedback: Correct. The announcement gives a time-sensitive action.
steps.hint: Find what the audience is expected to do.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A media message is always stated in one sentence at the top.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: False
steps.feedback: Correct. The message may come from the whole design.
steps.hint: Look at the full text, not just the title.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised reading words and images together.

quiz.title: What Is a Media Message? Quiz

questions.prompt: Which choice is a media text?
choices: a website page explaining summer reading
a keyboard used to type a website page
a camera used to take a website photo
questions.correctAnswer: a website page explaining summer reading
questions.reviewNote: The website page communicates a message.

questions.prompt: A classroom poster says, 'Return shared supplies after use.' What is the main message?
choices: Students should put shared supplies back.
The classroom has many supplies.
Some supplies are used during lessons.
questions.correctAnswer: Students should put shared supplies back.
questions.reviewNote: The poster gives a clear reminder.

questions.prompt: A sign says, 'Please wash hands before lunch.' What is the sign mostly doing?
choices: reminding people about a healthy routine
explaining the history of lunch
describing different handwashing sinks
questions.correctAnswer: reminding people about a healthy routine
questions.reviewNote: The sign asks people to follow a routine.

questions.prompt: A poster about a food drive shows cans being placed in a box. How does the image help?
choices: It shows what people are being asked to donate.
It lists every family taking part.
It explains how food is delivered to stores.
questions.correctAnswer: It shows what people are being asked to donate.

questions.prompt: On a map, a parking symbol marks a certain area. What does the symbol help readers do?
choices: find where parking is located
choose the best entrance to start from
know which route has the most traffic
questions.correctAnswer: find where parking is located

questions.prompt: A notice says, 'Permission forms are due Thursday.' What should the audience understand?
choices: Forms need to be handed in by Thursday.
Forms are usually printed on paper.
Thursday is part of the school week.
questions.correctAnswer: Forms need to be handed in by Thursday.

questions.prompt: Media texts can include posters, signs, websites, videos, and labels.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.reviewNote: These are all ways to communicate messages.

questions.prompt: Images in a media text can affect the message.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

lessons.title: Audience and Purpose
lessons.learningGoal: Students will identify the intended audience and purpose of media texts.
successCriteria: I can decide who a media text is made for.
I can identify whether a media text informs, persuades, entertains, or warns.
I can explain which clues helped me decide.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise using clues to identify the audience and purpose of media texts.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise using clues to identify the audience and purpose of media texts.
lessonContent: Audience means who a media text is meant for.
Purpose means why the media text was made.
A media text might inform, persuade, entertain, remind, warn, or invite.
Words, images, examples, and design can all give audience clues.
A good media reader explains which clues led to an answer.

Use the lesson quiz as a scored media literacy check.
Review missed questions before assigning the next Media Literacy and Digital Texts lesson.

studentActivity.title: Audience and Purpose Mission
studentActivity.mission: Use clues to decide who a media text is for and why it was made.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: media is made for someone
steps.text: A media creator makes choices for a particular audience. A poster for Grade 1 students will not sound exactly like a letter to parents.

steps.title: Use Clues
steps.prompt: Audience clues are everywhere
steps.text: Look at the vocabulary, examples, pictures, topic, and where the message appears. These clues help you decide who the creator had in mind.

steps.title: Audience Clue
steps.prompt: A flyer says, 'Parents and guardians are invited to meet the teachers at 6:30 p.m.' Who is the main audience?
choices: parents and guardians
students choosing a recess game
newspaper readers studying weather
steps.correctAnswer: parents and guardians
steps.feedback: Correct. The flyer names the audience directly.
steps.hint: Look for who is addressed.

steps.title: Age Fit
steps.prompt: Which media text is most likely meant for younger children?
choices: a picture chart showing how to tie shoes step by step
a student handbook page about attendance routines
a family newsletter about school readiness
steps.correctAnswer: a picture chart showing how to tie shoes step by step
steps.feedback: Yes. The topic and pictures fit younger children.
steps.hint: Think about what the audience needs.

steps.title: Audience Detail
steps.prompt: A sports camp website includes prices, drop-off times, and registration forms. Who needs that information most?
choices: families deciding whether to register a child
players learning a new warm-up drill
students writing a report about sports
steps.correctAnswer: families deciding whether to register a child
steps.feedback: Correct. Those details help families make a decision.
steps.hint: Ask who would use the information.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: The same topic can be explained differently for different audiences.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Audience affects wording and detail.
steps.hint: Audience changes choices.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised identifying audiences.

steps.title: Purpose Is the Job
steps.prompt: What is the media text trying to do?
steps.text: A media text can have more than one purpose, but usually one purpose is strongest. It may inform people, persuade them, entertain them, or warn them.

steps.title: Inform
steps.prompt: A school website page lists the date, time, and location of the winter concert. What is its main purpose?
choices: to inform families about event details
to persuade students to join the choir
to entertain readers with a concert story
steps.correctAnswer: to inform families about event details
steps.feedback: Correct. It gives information people need.
steps.hint: Look for facts and details.

steps.title: Persuade
steps.prompt: A poster says, 'Join the cleanup team and help keep our playground ready for everyone.' What is its main purpose?
choices: to persuade students to join
to explain how playground equipment is built
to compare two different schoolyards
steps.correctAnswer: to persuade students to join
steps.feedback: Yes. It encourages action.
steps.hint: Look for a call to action.

steps.title: Warn
steps.prompt: A digital notice says, 'Do not share your password with anyone.' What is its main purpose?
choices: to warn users about online safety
to describe how passwords are made
to invite users to design a new login page
steps.correctAnswer: to warn users about online safety
steps.feedback: Correct. It gives a safety warning.
steps.hint: Safety messages often warn.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A media text can persuade politely without pressuring or misleading people.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Persuasion should still be fair.
steps.hint: Persuasion can be respectful.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised identifying purpose.

questions.prompt: A notice says, 'Families may book interview times online.' Who is the main audience?
choices: families of students
students choosing library books
people visiting a community museum
questions.correctAnswer: families of students

questions.prompt: Which detail is the strongest clue that a webpage is for students?
choices: It uses student login steps and class activity buttons.
It has a heading at the top of the page.
It uses a large button for one section.
questions.correctAnswer: It uses student login steps and class activity buttons.

questions.prompt: Which choice best fits directions for Grade 5 students?
choices: Use your notes to choose two facts that support your answer.
Copy the sentence starter before adding your answer.
Write a formal proposal with outside references.
questions.correctAnswer: Use your notes to choose two facts that support your answer.
questions.reviewNote: The task fits Grade 5 reading and writing.

questions.prompt: A schedule shows practice times and room numbers. What is the main purpose?
choices: to inform people where and when to go
to convince people to change the rooms
to tell a story about the team
questions.correctAnswer: to inform people where and when to go

questions.prompt: A class poster says, 'Bring one canned item to help stock the food shelf.' What is the purpose?
choices: to persuade people to donate
to explain where donation boxes are kept
to describe how the food shelf is organized
questions.correctAnswer: to persuade people to donate
questions.reviewNote: The poster asks for an action.

questions.prompt: A message says, 'Check with an adult before downloading a new app.' What is the purpose?
choices: to warn about safe digital choices
to describe where apps are stored
to advertise a school tablet
questions.correctAnswer: to warn about safe digital choices

questions.prompt: Audience means the people a media text is mainly meant to reach.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: Purpose means only the colour choices used in a media text.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.reviewNote: Purpose means why it was made.

lessons.title: Images, Layout, and Design Choices
lessons.learningGoal: Students will explain how visual and layout choices affect a media message.
successCriteria: I can identify design choices such as colour, size, placement, and spacing.
I can explain how an image supports or changes a message.
I can choose a layout that helps readers understand information.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise interpreting visual choices and choosing clear layouts for media texts.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise interpreting visual choices and choosing clear layouts for media texts.
lessonContent: Layout means how words, images, headings, and space are arranged.
Design choices can make information easier or harder to understand.
Large text, bold headings, and strong contrast can show importance.
Images should support the message, not distract from it.
Good design helps the audience find and understand information.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as a scored media literacy check.
Review missed questions before assigning the next Media Literacy and Digital Texts lesson.

studentActivityPlan.title: Design Choices Mission
studentActivityPlan.description: Choose design and layout choices that make media messages clearer.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Images, Layout, and Design Choices Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Layout, image support, emphasis, readability, and visual organization

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity for guided media literacy decisions and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Design Choices Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose design and layout choices that make media messages clearer.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: design affects meaning
steps.text: Design is part of the message. A large headline, a warning colour, a photograph, or a clear icon can guide what the audience notices first.

steps.title: Look at What Stands Out
steps.prompt: Emphasis guides attention
steps.text: When a media text makes something bigger, brighter, centred, or repeated, it may be showing that this part is important.

steps.title: Emphasis
steps.prompt: A poster puts 'Registration closes Friday' in the largest text. Why?
choices: The deadline is important for the audience to notice.
The designer wanted every sentence to look different.
The poster has no other way to include dates.
steps.correctAnswer: The deadline is important for the audience to notice.
steps.feedback: Correct. Larger text creates emphasis.
steps.hint: Ask why that part stands out.

steps.title: Image Choice
steps.prompt: Which image best supports a notice about bicycle safety?
choices: a child wearing a helmet while riding on a path
a close-up of a bicycle bell
a photo of many bikes in a shop window
steps.correctAnswer: a child wearing a helmet while riding on a path
steps.feedback: Yes. It directly supports the safety message.
steps.hint: Choose the image that matches the message.

steps.title: Colour Meaning
steps.prompt: A weather alert uses a strong red banner behind the warning. What effect does this likely have?
choices: It helps the warning feel urgent.
It shows the alert is only for adults.
It proves the forecast will be correct.
steps.correctAnswer: It helps the warning feel urgent.
steps.feedback: Correct. Colour can affect mood and importance.
steps.hint: Think about how the colour makes the message feel.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Images and layout can affect how people understand a media text.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Design is part of meaning.
steps.hint: Visual choices communicate.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised noticing design choices.

steps.title: Make It Easy to Read
steps.prompt: Good layout supports the audience
steps.text: A clear layout places information where readers can find it. Headings, spacing, lists, and labels can make a media text easier to use.

steps.title: Event Poster
steps.prompt: Which layout would help people understand a school concert poster?
choices: title at top, date and time together, location clearly labelled
small date in one corner, location inside a long paragraph, title at bottom
three different headings for the same event and no time listed
steps.correctAnswer: title at top, date and time together, location clearly labelled
steps.feedback: Correct. Important details are easy to find.
steps.hint: Choose the layout that helps the audience use the information.

steps.title: Website Button
steps.prompt: A website wants students to begin an activity. Which button label is clearest?
choices: Start Activity
Continue to the next learning area
Click here for possible steps
steps.correctAnswer: Start Activity
steps.feedback: Yes. It is short and direct.
steps.hint: Button labels should tell users what will happen.

steps.title: Readability
steps.prompt: Which design choice makes a digital poster easier to read?
choices: dark text on a light background with enough space
small pale text over a busy picture
four fonts changing every few words
steps.correctAnswer: dark text on a light background with enough space
steps.feedback: Correct. Contrast and spacing help readers.
steps.hint: Readability matters more than decoration.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A beautiful design can still be weak if the audience cannot find the important information.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Design should help communication.
steps.hint: Clear comes before fancy.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised choosing clear layouts.

quiz.title: Images, Layout, and Design Choices Quiz

questions.prompt: Why might a poster make one deadline larger than the rest of the text?
choices: to show it is important to notice
to make the poster use more space
to avoid using a heading
questions.correctAnswer: to show it is important to notice

questions.prompt: Which image best supports a poster about reading outside?
choices: students reading on a blanket under a tree
a stack of books beside a closed door
a school hallway after dismissal
questions.correctAnswer: students reading on a blanket under a tree

questions.prompt: Which layout is clearest for a field trip reminder?
choices: date, destination, items to bring, and return time in labelled sections
one paragraph mixing all details in any order
large title with most details in very small print
questions.correctAnswer: date, destination, items to bring, and return time in labelled sections

questions.prompt: Which button label is clearest for submitting a quiz?
choices: Submit Quiz
Finish with the thing
Move forward from here
questions.correctAnswer: Submit Quiz
questions.reviewNote: The label tells what will happen.

questions.prompt: Which design choice improves readability?
choices: clear contrast between text and background
decorative letters for every sentence
placing labels far from the items they name
questions.correctAnswer: clear contrast between text and background

questions.prompt: A poster is about washing hands before snack. Which image fits best?
choices: hands being washed at a sink
students sitting at desks with notebooks
a lunch bag beside a backpack
questions.correctAnswer: hands being washed at a sink

questions.prompt: Layout means how text, images, headings, and space are arranged.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: Design choices should never affect how a media message is understood.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.reviewNote: Design choices can strongly affect understanding.

lessons.title: Fact, Opinion, and Persuasion
lessons.learningGoal: Students will distinguish facts, opinions, and persuasive techniques in media texts.
successCriteria: I can identify a fact that can be checked.
I can identify an opinion or judgement.
I can notice persuasive words and decide whether support is strong.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise telling the difference between checkable facts, opinions, and persuasive messages.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise telling the difference between checkable facts, opinions, and persuasive messages.
lessonContent: A fact can be checked or proven.
An opinion tells what someone thinks, feels, believes, or prefers.
Persuasion tries to convince the audience to think, feel, choose, or do something.
Persuasive media should use fair reasons and evidence.
Careful readers ask whether a claim is supported.
practiceIdeas: Share the student mission for practice stars.
Use the lesson quiz as a scored media literacy check.
Review missed questions before assigning the next Media Literacy and Digital Texts lesson.

studentActivityPlan.title: Fact or Persuasion Mission
studentActivityPlan.description: Sort facts, opinions, and persuasive claims in media texts.
studentActivityPlan.reward: 10 practice stars after each completed level

quizPlan.title: Fact, Opinion, and Persuasion Quiz
quizPlan.format: Multiple choice and true/false questions with one score at the end.
quizPlan.focus: Facts, opinions, claims, evidence, persuasive wording, and fair support

lessons.assessmentPlan: Use the activity for guided media literacy decisions and the quiz to check independent understanding.

studentActivity.title: Fact or Persuasion Mission
studentActivity.mission: Sort facts, opinions, and persuasive claims in media texts.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: not every statement works the same way
steps.text: A media text may mix facts and opinions. The reader's job is to know which statements can be checked and which statements are judgements or preferences.

steps.title: Checkable or Judgement?
steps.prompt: Facts can be checked
steps.text: If a statement gives a date, number, location, or proven detail, it may be a fact. If it tells what is best, easiest, most exciting, or most beautiful, it is probably an opinion.

steps.title: Fact
steps.prompt: Which sentence is a fact?
choices: The school concert begins at 7:00 p.m.
The concert will be the best event of the year.
Everyone will enjoy the concert more than sports day.
steps.correctAnswer: The school concert begins at 7:00 p.m.
steps.feedback: Correct. The time can be checked.
steps.hint: Facts can be proven or checked.

steps.title: Opinion
steps.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion?
choices: The new playground design is more inviting than the old one.
The playground has two slides and one climbing wall.
The playground opened on Monday morning.
steps.correctAnswer: The new playground design is more inviting than the old one.
steps.feedback: Yes. It gives a judgement.
steps.hint: Opinions often use judgement words.

steps.title: Mixed Message
steps.prompt: A flyer says, 'The bake sale starts at 10:00. These treats are the tastiest way to support our team.' Which part is an opinion?
choices: These treats are the tastiest way to support our team.
The bake sale starts at 10:00.
The flyer is about a bake sale.
steps.correctAnswer: These treats are the tastiest way to support our team.
steps.feedback: Correct. Tastiest is a judgement.
steps.hint: Look for the part that cannot be proven for everyone.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A media text can include both facts and opinions.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Many media texts use both.
steps.hint: One text can do several things.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised sorting facts and opinions.

steps.title: Notice Persuasion
steps.prompt: Persuasion tries to convince
steps.text: Persuasive media may use strong words, emotional pictures, examples, promises, or reasons. A careful reader asks whether the message is fair and supported.

steps.title: Persuasive Claim
steps.prompt: Which sentence is trying to persuade?
choices: Choose the library helper club if you want to make reading time better for younger students.
The library helper club meets on Tuesdays after lunch.
The library helper club has eight members this term.
steps.correctAnswer: Choose the library helper club if you want to make reading time better for younger students.
steps.feedback: Correct. It encourages a choice.
steps.hint: Persuasion often asks people to act.

steps.title: Strong Support
steps.prompt: Claim: A walking school bus would help students arrive safely. Which support is strongest?
choices: Students would walk in a supervised group on planned routes.
Walking can happen in many neighbourhoods.
Some students already own comfortable shoes.
steps.correctAnswer: Students would walk in a supervised group on planned routes.
steps.feedback: Yes. It explains how safety would improve.
steps.hint: Strong support connects directly to the claim.

steps.title: Weak Support
steps.prompt: Claim: Our class should use labelled recycling bins. Which support is weakest?
choices: The labels could be printed on white paper.
Labels would help students sort paper, plastic, and cans correctly.
Clear bin signs would reduce mistakes during cleanup.
steps.correctAnswer: The labels could be printed on white paper.
steps.feedback: Correct. It mentions labels but does not strongly support the claim.
steps.hint: Weak support may be related but not convincing.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A persuasive message is stronger when it uses reasons that can be checked or explained.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Support matters.
steps.hint: Persuasion should not rely only on strong feelings.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised finding persuasive support.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a fact?
choices: The museum opens at 9:30 a.m.
The museum would be a useful trip choice for our class.
The museum exhibits seem easier to understand than the website.
questions.correctAnswer: The museum opens at 9:30 a.m.
questions.reviewNote: The opening time can be checked.

questions.prompt: Which statement is an opinion?
choices: The poster uses a photograph of a school garden.
The garden club meets every second Wednesday.
The garden club is the best way to spend recess.
questions.correctAnswer: The garden club is the best way to spend recess.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is opinion in this sentence: 'The race begins at 2:00, and it will be the most exciting race yet'?
choices: it will be the most exciting race yet
The race begins at 2:00
race begins
questions.correctAnswer: it will be the most exciting race yet

questions.prompt: Which sentence is most persuasive?
choices: Join the reading challenge and help our class reach its goal.
The reading challenge begins next week.
Students may record books on a chart.
questions.correctAnswer: Join the reading challenge and help our class reach its goal.
questions.reviewNote: It asks the audience to join.

questions.prompt: Claim: Bike racks should be added near the front door. Which support is strongest?
choices: More students could lock bikes in a visible, organized place.
Bike racks can be made from metal.
The front door is where many people enter.
questions.correctAnswer: More students could lock bikes in a visible, organized place.

questions.prompt: Claim: The class should use reusable containers. Which support is weakest?
choices: Some containers have colourful lids.
Reusable containers can reduce daily garbage.
Families can wash and use the same containers again.
questions.correctAnswer: Some containers have colourful lids.
questions.reviewNote: It is related but not strong support.

questions.prompt: A fact can be checked or proven.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: Persuasive media should be read carefully to see whether the claim is supported.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

lessons.title: Online Information and Credibility
lessons.learningGoal: Students will evaluate whether online information seems useful, current, and trustworthy.
successCriteria: I can check who made or published online information.
I can decide whether a source fits my question.
I can notice clues that information may need to be checked with another source.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise safe, age-appropriate habits for judging online information.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise safe, age-appropriate habits for judging online information.
lessonContent: Credible information is trustworthy enough to use after careful checking.
Online readers should ask who made the information and why it was made.
A source should fit the question being researched.
Dates can matter because some information changes over time.
Important information should be checked with more than one reliable source.

studentActivity.title: Online Source Checker
studentActivity.mission: Choose online information habits that help readers check sources carefully.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: online information needs checking
steps.text: Online information can be helpful, but not everything online is equally reliable. A careful reader checks the source before trusting or sharing information.

steps.title: Who Made It?
steps.prompt: Look for source clues
steps.text: Check whether the page names an author, organization, date, and purpose. These clues help you decide whether the information is useful for your question.

steps.title: Author
steps.prompt: Which source clue is most helpful when deciding whether to trust an article about local weather safety?
choices: the article is published by the city's emergency information page
the article uses a large weather photograph
the article has a short title that is easy to remember
steps.correctAnswer: the article is published by the city's emergency information page
steps.feedback: Correct. The publisher connects to the topic.
steps.hint: Ask who is responsible for the information.

steps.title: Date
steps.prompt: You are checking school bus cancellation information. Which date matters most?
choices: today's update date
the date the website was first designed
the date of last year's winter break
steps.correctAnswer: today's update date
steps.feedback: Yes. Current information matters for bus cancellations.
steps.hint: Some information changes quickly.

steps.title: Purpose
steps.prompt: A webpage about a snack says many good things about one brand and has a 'Buy Now' button. What should readers notice?
choices: the page may be trying to sell the snack
the page may be written for families choosing snacks
the page may include facts mixed with advertising
steps.correctAnswer: the page may be trying to sell the snack
steps.feedback: Correct. Selling can affect the message.
steps.hint: Look at why the page was made.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: The person or group behind online information can affect how trustworthy it is.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Source matters.
steps.hint: Who made it is an important clue.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised checking source clues.

steps.title: Fit and Verify
steps.prompt: Use more than one clue
steps.text: A source can look polished but still not answer your question. A careful reader checks whether the source fits, whether the information is current, and whether another reliable source agrees.

steps.title: Source Fit
steps.prompt: Question: How do maple trees produce sap? Which source fits best?
choices: a science article about maple sap and tree growth
a recipe page for maple cookies
a travel page about fall colours in Canada
steps.correctAnswer: a science article about maple sap and tree growth
steps.feedback: Correct. It directly answers the question.
steps.hint: Match the source to the research question.

steps.title: Verify
steps.prompt: A website gives a surprising fact for a science report, but it does not name an author or source. What should a student do?
choices: check the fact with another reliable source
use it only if it fits the report question
save the page and look for the date first
steps.correctAnswer: check the fact with another reliable source
steps.feedback: Yes. Important information should be checked.
steps.hint: Surprising claims deserve careful checking.

steps.title: Outdated
steps.prompt: A page from 2014 lists current tablet prices for students. What is the main concern?
choices: the prices may be outdated
the page uses numbers
the topic includes technology
steps.correctAnswer: the prices may be outdated
steps.feedback: Correct. Prices and technology information can change.
steps.hint: Dates matter when information changes.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A source can look attractive and still need careful checking.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Design alone does not prove accuracy.
steps.hint: Do not judge only by looks.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised checking online credibility.

questions.prompt: Which source is likely strongest for school weather closure information?
choices: the school board's official update page
a student's old slideshow about winter
a general article about snow activities
questions.correctAnswer: the school board's official update page
questions.reviewNote: The official page fits the information need.

questions.prompt: Why does the date matter for a webpage about bus routes?
choices: routes may change over time
the page may use last term's school schedule
the route names may look similar each year
questions.correctAnswer: routes may change over time

questions.prompt: A page praises one backpack brand and includes a shopping link. What is a careful reader's best thought?
choices: The page may be trying to sell the backpack.
The page must be a neutral school report.
The page cannot include any useful facts.
questions.correctAnswer: The page may be trying to sell the backpack.
questions.reviewNote: A selling purpose can shape the message.

questions.prompt: Question: Why do leaves change colour in fall? Which source fits best?
choices: a science article about pigments in leaves
a craft page about leaf rubbings
a photo gallery of autumn parks
questions.correctAnswer: a science article about pigments in leaves

questions.prompt: What should a student do with an important online fact that appears in only one unclear source?
choices: check it with another reliable source
include it because one source is enough
make the title more exciting
questions.correctAnswer: check it with another reliable source

questions.prompt: Which clue helps readers judge credibility?
choices: the page names the author or organization
the page has a bright button
the page loads quickly on a tablet
questions.correctAnswer: the page names the author or organization
questions.reviewNote: The author or organization is an important clue.

questions.prompt: Online information should be checked before it is used for important work.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: A polished website design automatically proves the information is accurate.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False

lessons.title: Digital Citizenship and Respectful Communication
lessons.learningGoal: Students will choose safe, respectful, and responsible ways to communicate online.
successCriteria: I can identify private information that should not be shared online.
I can choose respectful wording for digital communication.
I can decide when to ask a trusted adult for help.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise wise and respectful digital communication habits.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise wise and respectful digital communication habits.
lessonContent: Digital citizenship means using technology responsibly and respectfully.
Private information should be protected.
Online messages should be truthful, kind, and clear.
Pictures, names, and personal details should not be shared without permission.
If something online feels unsafe or confusing, students should ask a trusted adult for help.

studentActivity.title: Digital Citizenship Mission
studentActivity.mission: Choose safe and respectful responses for common digital situations.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: protect private information
steps.text: Digital tools can be useful for learning, but students need wise habits. Some information belongs only with family, teachers, or trusted adults.

steps.title: Think Before Sharing
steps.prompt: Permission matters
steps.text: Before sharing someone's picture, name, work, or personal details online, ask whether you have permission. When unsure, ask a trusted adult.

steps.title: Private Information
steps.prompt: Which detail should a student avoid posting in a public class comment?
choices: home address
favourite school subject
first name only
steps.correctAnswer: home address
steps.feedback: Correct. A home address is private.
steps.hint: Choose the detail that could identify where someone lives.

steps.title: Permission
steps.prompt: A student wants to post a photo of classmates from a project. What should happen first?
choices: check with the teacher or get permission
post it quickly before anyone leaves
add more classmates to make the photo better
steps.correctAnswer: check with the teacher or get permission
steps.feedback: Yes. Photos of others need care.
steps.hint: Permission protects people.

steps.title: Trusted Adult
steps.prompt: A message from an unknown person asks a student for personal information. What should the student do?
choices: stop and tell a trusted adult
answer only one question
ask the person to explain first
steps.correctAnswer: stop and tell a trusted adult
steps.feedback: Correct. Students should get help.
steps.hint: Unknown requests need adult help.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Students should protect private information when using digital tools.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Privacy matters.
steps.hint: Personal details need care.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised privacy and permission choices.

steps.title: Words Still Matter Online
steps.prompt: Digital messages should be respectful
steps.text: Online writing can feel quick, but it still affects real people. Respectful messages are clear, honest, and kind, even when people disagree.

steps.title: Respectful Reply
steps.prompt: Which reply is most respectful after a classmate shares an idea online?
choices: I disagree because the evidence points to a different answer.
That answer cannot be right because I dislike it.
Your idea should be replaced with mine.
steps.correctAnswer: I disagree because the evidence points to a different answer.
steps.feedback: Correct. It disagrees with a reason and respect.
steps.hint: Respectful disagreement explains the idea, not the person.

steps.title: Tone
steps.prompt: Which message has the clearest helpful tone?
choices: Could you please add the source for this fact?
You forgot the source again.
The source part is missing, so this is not useful.
steps.correctAnswer: Could you please add the source for this fact?
steps.feedback: Yes. It is clear and respectful.
steps.hint: Helpful tone asks or explains without shaming.

steps.title: Slow Down
steps.prompt: A student feels angry after reading a comment. What is the wisest next step?
choices: pause before replying and ask for help if needed
send a quick reply while still angry
copy the message to more classmates
steps.correctAnswer: pause before replying and ask for help if needed
steps.feedback: Correct. Pausing helps prevent unwise replies.
steps.hint: Strong feelings are a good time to slow down.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Respectful online communication can still include disagreement.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Disagreement can be respectful.
steps.hint: Respect is about how ideas are expressed.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised responsible digital communication.

quiz.title: Digital Citizenship and Respectful Communication Quiz

questions.prompt: Which detail should not be shared in a public online comment?
choices: home address
book title being discussed
the name of a school subject
questions.correctAnswer: home address

questions.prompt: Before posting a photo of classmates, what should a student do?
choices: ask the teacher or get permission
crop the photo without telling anyone
post it only if the picture is clear
questions.correctAnswer: ask the teacher or get permission

questions.prompt: What should a student do if an unknown person asks for personal details online?
choices: tell a trusted adult
answer with shorter details
move the conversation to another app
questions.correctAnswer: tell a trusted adult

questions.prompt: Which comment is most respectful?
choices: I see your point, but the paragraph gives different evidence.
Your answer is not worth using.
Everyone should choose my answer instead.
questions.correctAnswer: I see your point, but the paragraph gives different evidence.

questions.prompt: Which reply is most helpful for peer feedback?
choices: Your main idea is clear; adding one example would make it stronger.
It needs work.
I would write it differently.
questions.correctAnswer: Your main idea is clear; adding one example would make it stronger.
questions.reviewNote: It gives a specific strength and next step.

questions.prompt: What is wise before replying to an upsetting online comment?
choices: pause and think before responding
reply immediately so the feeling is clear
send the comment to several friends first
questions.correctAnswer: pause and think before responding

questions.prompt: Private information should be protected online.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: Online messages should be respectful because real people read them.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

lessons.title: Comparing Media Texts
lessons.learningGoal: Students will compare how two media texts communicate similar topics in different ways.
successCriteria: I can identify what two media texts have in common.
I can compare audience, purpose, and design choices.
I can explain which text is stronger for a particular job.
lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise comparing media texts by audience, purpose, message, and design choices.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise comparing media texts by audience, purpose, message, and design choices.
lessonContent: Two media texts can be about the same topic but communicate differently.
Comparing means noticing what is similar and what is different.
Media texts can differ in audience, purpose, wording, images, and layout.
A text is effective when its choices help it do its job well.
The stronger text depends on the purpose and audience.

studentActivity.title: Media Compare Mission
studentActivity.mission: Compare media texts and decide which choices fit the audience and purpose best.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: same topic, different choices
steps.text: Two media texts may both be about reading, recycling, safety, or an event. They can still use different words, images, and designs because they are made for different audiences or purposes.

steps.title: Use Fair Comparisons
steps.prompt: Compare the same features
steps.text: Good comparisons look at message, audience, purpose, design, and evidence. Do not just say one is better; explain why one works better for a certain job.

steps.title: Similar Topic
steps.prompt: Text A is a school poster asking students to join the choir. Text B is an email giving parents choir concert details. What do they have in common?
choices: Both are about choir.
Both are mainly asking students to register.
Both are written for parents only.
steps.correctAnswer: Both are about choir.
steps.feedback: Correct. The topic is shared.
steps.hint: Find the common topic first.

steps.title: Different Audience
steps.prompt: How are the choir poster and parent email different?
choices: They are made for different audiences.
They must have the same purpose.
They cannot share any information.
steps.correctAnswer: They are made for different audiences.
steps.feedback: Yes. One is for students and one is for parents.
steps.hint: Audience can change the message.

steps.title: Purpose Difference
steps.prompt: One recycling poster says, 'Sort waste correctly.' Another chart shows which items go in each bin. How are their purposes different?
choices: The poster reminds or persuades; the chart gives detailed guidance.
The poster is about science; the chart is about art.
The chart tries to sell recycling bins.
steps.correctAnswer: The poster reminds or persuades; the chart gives detailed guidance.
steps.feedback: Correct. They help in different ways.
steps.hint: Think about the job each text does.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Two media texts can share a topic but have different audiences.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Topic and audience are not the same.
steps.hint: Same topic does not mean same audience.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised comparing message and audience.

steps.title: Which Works Better?
steps.prompt: Effectiveness depends on the job
steps.text: A colourful poster may work well to catch attention. A detailed webpage may work better for directions. The best choice depends on what the audience needs.

steps.title: Best for Quick Reminder
steps.prompt: Which media text is best for reminding students quickly to bring indoor shoes tomorrow?
choices: a short poster by the classroom door
a long article about winter footwear
a slideshow about shoe manufacturing
steps.correctAnswer: a short poster by the classroom door
steps.feedback: Correct. A quick reminder should be easy to see.
steps.hint: Match the text to the purpose.

steps.title: Best for Details
steps.prompt: Which media text is best for families who need field trip cost, timing, lunch details, and permission information?
choices: a detailed email with labelled sections
a hallway poster with one large picture
a short slogan on a bookmark
steps.correctAnswer: a detailed email with labelled sections
steps.feedback: Yes. Families need several specific details.
steps.hint: Details need space and organization.

steps.title: Design Choice
steps.prompt: Two food drive posters have the same facts. Poster A uses clear headings and a photo of donation boxes. Poster B uses small text in one crowded paragraph. Which is likely more effective?
choices: Poster A, because the information is easier to find.
Poster B, because crowded text includes more words.
They are equally effective because facts are the same.
steps.correctAnswer: Poster A, because the information is easier to find.
steps.feedback: Correct. Design affects usefulness.
steps.hint: Effectiveness includes readability.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: The most effective media text is the one that best fits its audience and purpose.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Fit matters.
steps.hint: Effective means it does its job well.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised comparing media effectiveness.

questions.prompt: A poster invites students to chess club. An email tells parents chess club pickup time. What do they have in common?
choices: Both are about chess club.
Both are written mainly for parents.
Both give pickup instructions only.
questions.correctAnswer: Both are about chess club.

questions.prompt: A lunch menu with pictures is posted for students. A nutrition newsletter is sent to families. How are they different?
choices: They are made for different audiences.
They cannot include the same foods.
They must use the same amount of detail.
questions.correctAnswer: They are made for different audiences.

questions.prompt: A safety poster says, 'Walk in the hallway.' A handbook page explains all hallway rules. How are their purposes different?
choices: The poster gives a quick reminder; the handbook gives fuller details.
The handbook is persuasive; the poster is a story.
The poster is only for teachers; the handbook is only for visitors.
questions.correctAnswer: The poster gives a quick reminder; the handbook gives fuller details.

questions.prompt: Which text is best for a quick reminder about tomorrow's library books?
choices: a short classroom notice
a long research report
a detailed website privacy policy
questions.correctAnswer: a short classroom notice
questions.reviewNote: A quick reminder should be easy to see.

questions.prompt: Which text is best for explaining how to complete an online assignment?
choices: a step-by-step guide with screenshots
a poster with only the assignment title
a short announcement over the speaker
questions.correctAnswer: a step-by-step guide with screenshots

questions.prompt: Which media text is more effective for a map of a school fair?
choices: a labelled map with entrances, activity areas, and washrooms
a paragraph describing every table in order
a poster with only the fair title and date
questions.correctAnswer: a labelled map with entrances, activity areas, and washrooms
questions.reviewNote: A map should help people find places.

questions.prompt: Comparing media texts means noticing similarities and differences.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

questions.prompt: A media text can be strong for one audience and less useful for another.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

lessons.teacherOverview: Students practise planning and checking a simple media message before sharing it.
lessons.teacherSummary: Students practise planning and checking a simple media message before sharing it.
lessonContent: Creating media begins with audience and purpose.
Words, images, layout, and design should all support the same message.
A media creator should be truthful and respectful.
The message should be easy for the audience to understand.
Revision helps improve clarity before the media text is shared.

studentActivity.title: Create a Media Message Mission
studentActivity.mission: Plan and revise simple media messages that fit the audience and purpose.

steps.title: Before You Begin
steps.prompt: Get ready: plan before creating
steps.text: A media message works best when the creator knows the audience and purpose first. Then every choice can support the same message.

steps.title: Choose Fitting Parts
steps.prompt: Words, images, and layout should agree
steps.text: If your message asks students to bring library books, the title, image, date, and button or reminder should all point to that job.

steps.title: Audience
steps.prompt: A student is making a poster to remind Grade 5 classmates about a science fair deadline. Which audience should guide the choices?
choices: Grade 5 classmates
families reading the school newsletter
students visiting the science fair later
steps.correctAnswer: Grade 5 classmates
steps.feedback: Correct. The poster is for Grade 5 classmates.
steps.hint: Use the audience named in the task.

steps.title: Purpose
steps.prompt: What is the purpose of a poster that says, 'Bring your science fair display board by Monday'?
choices: to remind students about a deadline
to explain every step of the science fair
to entertain students with a science story
steps.correctAnswer: to remind students about a deadline
steps.feedback: Yes. It gives a clear reminder.
steps.hint: Ask what the poster wants people to do.

steps.title: Image Choice
steps.prompt: Which image best fits a poster about bringing a reusable lunch container?
choices: a lunch container beside a lunch bag
a lunch table with students eating
a school backpack packed for the day
steps.correctAnswer: a lunch container beside a lunch bag
steps.feedback: Correct. The image supports the message.
steps.hint: Choose the image that matches the action.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: A simple media message should have a clear audience and purpose.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Planning matters.
steps.hint: Audience and purpose guide choices.

steps.title: Level 1 Complete
steps.prompt: You practised planning media messages.

steps.title: Review Before Sharing
steps.prompt: Creators are responsible
steps.text: Before sharing a media message, check that it is accurate, respectful, readable, and complete. If something might confuse the audience, revise it.

steps.title: Truthfulness
steps.prompt: A poster says, 'Every participant will win a prize,' but only ten prizes are available. What should the creator do?
choices: revise the message so it is accurate
change the poster to say prizes are limited
ask whether the teacher can add more prizes
steps.correctAnswer: revise the message so it is accurate
steps.feedback: Correct. Media messages should be truthful.
steps.hint: Accuracy matters before sharing.

steps.title: Readable Layout
steps.prompt: Which revision would make a poster easier to use?
choices: put the date, time, and place in a clear list
add three more background pictures
make the title use several different fonts
steps.correctAnswer: put the date, time, and place in a clear list
steps.feedback: Yes. A list helps the audience find details.
steps.hint: Choose the revision that improves clarity.

steps.title: Respectful Message
steps.prompt: Which slogan is best for a poster encouraging careful tablet use?
choices: Use tablets wisely so everyone can learn.
Careless tablet use slows learning for the class.
Good tablet habits help devices last longer.
steps.correctAnswer: Use tablets wisely so everyone can learn.
steps.feedback: Correct. It is positive and respectful.
steps.hint: A strong message can still be respectful.

steps.title: True or False
steps.prompt: Creators should revise a media message if the audience might misunderstand it.
choices: True
False
steps.correctAnswer: True
steps.feedback: Correct. Revision improves communication.
steps.hint: Clear communication matters.

steps.title: Mission Complete
steps.prompt: You practised creating and revising media messages.

questions.prompt: A poster is made to remind Grade 5 students about indoor shoes. Who is the main audience?
choices: Grade 5 students
families buying winter coats
teachers planning report cards
questions.correctAnswer: Grade 5 students
questions.reviewNote: The poster is for Grade 5 students.

questions.prompt: A message says, 'Sign up for the class cleanup team by Thursday.' What is its purpose?
choices: to persuade students to sign up by a deadline
to explain how cleaners are trained
to compare two classroom jobs
questions.correctAnswer: to persuade students to sign up by a deadline

questions.prompt: Which image best supports a poster about returning library books?

a student writing a math answer

questions.prompt: Which layout helps readers understand an event poster?

title and picture only, with details in tiny print

questions.correctAnswer: event name, date, time, place, and what to bring clearly separated
questions.reviewNote: Important details are easy to find.

questions.prompt: A flyer says a club meets every Friday, but it meets every second Friday. What should the creator do?
choices: correct the schedule before sharing
leave it because the flyer looks finished
add more pictures instead of changing the words
questions.correctAnswer: correct the schedule before sharing

questions.prompt: A poster has a good message but the date is hard to find. What revision fits best?
choices: make the date easy to see near the main reminder
move the date into the paragraph below the title
add a second picture to balance the layout
questions.correctAnswer: make the date easy to see near the main reminder

questions.prompt: A media creator should check that the message is truthful and respectful.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False

lessons.title: Unit 5 Final Quiz

lessons.teacherSummary: The Unit 5 final quiz checks media messages, audience and purpose, design choices, fact and opinion, persuasion, online credibility, digital citizenship, media comparison, and media creation.

quiz.title: Media Literacy and Digital Texts Unit Quiz

questions.prompt: Which choice is a media text?
choices: a poster advertising a school play
a printer used to make theatre programs
a box used to store stage supplies
questions.correctAnswer: a poster advertising a school play

questions.prompt: A notice says, 'Bring your recorder for music class on Tuesday.' What is the main message?
choices: Students need their recorders on Tuesday.
Music class includes instruments.
Tuesday is part of the school schedule.
questions.correctAnswer: Students need their recorders on Tuesday.
questions.reviewNote: The notice tells students what to bring and when.

questions.prompt: A webpage has student activity buttons, practice stars, and a class code login. Who is the main audience?
choices: students using the learning site
parents paying school fees
teachers writing report cards
questions.correctAnswer: students using the learning site

questions.prompt: A poster says, 'Join the lunchtime walking club.' What is its main purpose?
choices: to persuade students to join
to explain how shoes are made
to compare gym and outdoor games
questions.correctAnswer: to persuade students to join

questions.prompt: A poster makes 'Forms due Friday' larger than the other text. Why?
choices: to help the audience notice the deadline
to make the poster look longer
to show the date is less important
questions.correctAnswer: to help the audience notice the deadline

questions.prompt: Which layout is clearest for a field trip reminder?
choices: date, place, cost, and what to bring in labelled sections
one long paragraph with details mixed together
a large picture with the time placed in tiny print
questions.correctAnswer: date, place, cost, and what to bring in labelled sections
questions.reviewNote: Labels help the audience find information.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a fact?
choices: The school fair starts at 5:30 p.m.
The fair will be the best event of spring.
The fair games are more fun than the food table.
questions.correctAnswer: The school fair starts at 5:30 p.m.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is an opinion?
choices: The new poster is more eye-catching than the old one.
The poster has three headings.
The poster was printed on Monday.
questions.correctAnswer: The new poster is more eye-catching than the old one.

questions.prompt: Claim: Our class should use a homework checklist. Which support is strongest?
choices: A checklist can help students remember each part before handing work in.
Checklists can be printed on half sheets.
Many classrooms have paper near the printer.
questions.correctAnswer: A checklist can help students remember each part before handing work in.
questions.reviewNote: It explains why the checklist would help.

questions.prompt: Which source is likely strongest for current school event dates?
choices: the official school website listing current dates
a classroom newsletter from last term
a student's paragraph about favourite school events
questions.correctAnswer: the official school website listing current dates
questions.reviewNote: The official website fits the need.

questions.prompt: A website gives a surprising health fact but does not say where it came from. What should a student do?
choices: check another reliable source or ask a trusted adult
use it only if it matches the paragraph topic
write it down and look for the page date
questions.correctAnswer: check another reliable source or ask a trusted adult

questions.prompt: Which information should not be posted in a public class comment?
choices: home address
favourite book genre
first name only
questions.correctAnswer: home address

questions.prompt: Which online reply is most respectful?
choices: I see your idea, but the evidence supports a different answer.
Your answer should be ignored.
My answer is better, so use it.
questions.correctAnswer: I see your idea, but the evidence supports a different answer.
questions.reviewNote: It disagrees with respect and a reason.

questions.prompt: A student poster invites classmates to a club. A parent email gives pickup details. How are they different?
choices: They are made for different audiences.
They cannot be about the same club.
They must use the same amount of detail.
questions.correctAnswer: They are made for different audiences.

questions.prompt: Which media text is best for helping visitors find booths at a school fair?
choices: a labelled map of the fair area
a slogan about fair day
a paragraph listing last year's events
questions.correctAnswer: a labelled map of the fair area
questions.reviewNote: A map fits the audience need.

questions.prompt: Before creating a media message, what should the creator decide first?
choices: audience and purpose
the number of decorations
where to put the smallest text
questions.correctAnswer: audience and purpose
questions.reviewNote: Audience and purpose guide every choice.

questions.prompt: A poster lists an incorrect start time for an event. What should the creator do?
choices: correct the time before sharing
move the time closer to the title
ask someone to check the design colours
questions.correctAnswer: correct the time before sharing

questions.prompt: A media text can use words, images, layout, and symbols to communicate.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.reviewNote: Media messages can use many features.

questions.prompt: A polished website design proves the information is correct.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: False

questions.prompt: Respectful online communication can include disagreement.
choices: True
False
questions.correctAnswer: True

unitGradePlan.note: Final Media Literacy and Digital Texts mark recommendation: 60% unit quiz and 40% average of lesson quizzes.

unitAssessmentPlan.lessonQuizzes: Each lesson has a short scored quiz to check the lesson focus.
unitAssessmentPlan.unitTest: The final unit quiz checks media messages, audience and purpose, design choices, fact and opinion, persuasion, online credibility, digital citizenship, comparing media texts, and creating a simple media message.
